1:
The date divides them. Keil and Delitzsch report that the fathers took the psalm to prophesy the wars of the Maccabees, and answer that it is explicable from the strengthened national self-consciousness of the period after Cyrus, its standpoint about that of the book of Esther; they place it in the restoration and assign it to the same hand as the psalm before it. Adam Clarke takes the older view, calling it a song of triumph probably from the time of the Maccabees, and notes that it has no title in the Hebrew or any version and no author’s name. Charles Ellicott agrees, arguing from the term for the congregation, by that age a regular title for the patriotic party. John Calvin puts it at the return from captivity and reads it as encouragement to expect the full deliverance of which the permission to return was only a prelude, the Spirit furnishing beforehand a remedy for the tyranny to come.

Keil and Delitzsch then do what none of the others do: they warn against the psalm. The New Testament church, they say, cannot pray as the Old Testament national church here prays, and under the illusion that it might be used as a prayer without spiritual transmutation this psalm has become the watchword of the most horrible errors; they begin to name the man who so used it, and the block breaks off mid-name.

The new song is read four ways. Augustine of Hippo makes it the difference between two men: the old man has an old song and the new man a new one, and whoever loves earthly things sings an old song however new his words; the new song is of peace and charity, so that whoever severs himself from the union of the saints has followed old strife, and whoever does not sing with the whole earth sings an old song, though his tongue sound the alleluia all day; his ears, he says, are not so much bent to hear the voice of the singer as to seek the deeds of the doer. Clarke takes new to mean excellent, the best song we can pronounce, supporting it from Latin usage with a line of a Latin poet and a gloss that the word there means great and admirable, then rounds on the poet’s English translator for a version he calls tame and inexpressive. Matthew Henry makes it new by occasion and by affection, sung with new affections that make the song new though the words have been used before, and keep them from growing threadbare. C.H. Spurgeon makes it a duty of invention: it is well to repeat the old and more useful to invent the new, men being fonder of new complaints than new psalms.

The dance is removed by three of them and kept by one for an unexpected reason. Clarke denies that the word ever means dancing anywhere in the Bible, holding that it and its cognate always signify a pipe, citing a lexicographer who derives it from a root meaning to make a hole. Ellicott reaches the same rendering by four arguments: the word appears in a list of orchestral instruments in the next psalm, one derivation favours it, an eastern version renders it by the name of a flute still found there, and its pairing with the drum answers to our pipe and tabor. John Gill allows the dance as an ancient practice but prefers the rendering with the pipe. Henry keeps the dance and uses it against instrumental music: those who urge music from this verse must by the same rule introduce dancing, since the two went together, whereas the New Testament keeps up singing as an ordinance and provides nothing for music and dancing. Gill and Henry both notice that the word for Maker in the next verse is plural, Henry finding in it the mystery of the Trinity.
4:
The beautifying of the meek is taken four ways in four sentences. Adam Clarke renders the verb as making fair and the noun as the lowly, and then reports a Latin father who translated the line as an exalting of the meek in Jesus; whether that rendering be correct or not, Clarke says, there is no other way by which the humble soul can be exalted. Charles Ellicott keeps the scene military and makes it literal: he adorns the oppressed with salvation, the honour won in the sight of the world being like a beautiful robe, a figure no doubt suggested by the actual triumphal dresses of the victors, or by the spoils in which they appeared after the battle. John Wesley makes it reputation, God adorning them so as to make them amiable and honourable in the eyes of a world that now hates and despises them. John Gill keeps to the pleasure God takes in them, in their persons as accepted in Christ, in their services offered in faith, and in their prosperity.

The beds of the next verse are turned into couches by two of them. Clarke reads the singing as done reclining at a festal banquet, where the praises of the Lord are to be shouted, and adds a scene from his own day: at public entertainments a Latin line from another psalm, giving the glory not to us but to God’s name for his mercy and truth, is often sung to the same purpose, so that feasting is mingled with divine songs; he adds that reclining on couches while taking food is still practised in eastern countries. Ellicott offers both possibilities without deciding, that the rejoicing may be carried far into the night so that the happy people burst out anew into singing after they have retired to rest, or that the couches may rather be the divans on which feasts were held.

Gill spends his space on the glory the saints are to be joyful in, taking it of the glory put upon them now, the righteousness of Christ upon them and his grace within them, and of the glory expected hereafter for body and soul. He reports that some copies of one ancient version read not in glory but in his glory, which would make the object the glory of Christ as seen now in the glass of the Gospel and to be seen then face to face; and he allows a third possibility, that the word is adverbial and means simply gloriously, in a glorious manner. Clarke reaches the same adverbial sense in three words, that they should be gloriously joyful, seeing themselves so honoured and so successful.
6:
Two commentators at opposite ends of the psalm warn against the use made of it. Keil and Delitzsch had said at the opening that the New Testament church cannot pray as the Old Testament national church here prays. Adam Clarke, at the closing verse, puts the question himself and answers it: do these last verses contain a promise that all the nations of the earth shall be brought under the dominion of the Church, that all heathen and ungodly kings shall be put down and pious men put in their places? He does not think so. He believes God never intended that his Church should have the civil government of the world, and that the Church, like its Founder and Head, will never be a ruler and divider among men.

Clarke defuses the militancy in three further ways. He sets the passage among the builders of the wall, where every man wrought with one hand and held a weapon with the other, so that the sword is defensive. He makes the punishments upon the people fall not on foreigners but on the unfaithful and treacherous of their own nation, some of whose nobles had joined the enemies of the work and made alliances contrary to the law. And where the psalm binds kings with chains he keeps the mood conditional, that if those kings and governors had attacked, God would have enabled his people to defeat them and lead their generals in triumph; the later victories he allows only as a possible reference, adding that the psalmist may speak of them in a hyperbolical way not unusual in songs of triumph.

John Gill takes the opposite route and spiritualises the whole armoury. The vengeance on the heathen becomes the apostles going out with the two-edged sword of the word, so that the oracles were struck dumb, the priests despised and the temples forsaken; and then, in the latter days, vengeance on Rome for idolatry, superstition and the blood of the saints. The kings bound with chains become emperors brought to the churches in chains of efficacious grace, and he names two of them, adding that they became instruments in destroying persecuting princes. Matthew Henry keeps the history but reads the verse as a job description: those who taught Israel the high praises of the Lord did also put a two-edged sword into their hand, and he instances the leader of the exodus, the captain who took the land, and the king who was at once the sweet singer of Israel and the captain of its hosts, teaching their hands to war as God had taught his. John Wesley keeps it plainest, the vengeance being literally accomplished by that king upon the neighbouring nations.

The philology is small but sharp. Charles Ellicott renders the high praises literally as exaltations of celebration, that is hymns of praise, and corrects the mouth to the throat, as Gill also does. Clarke observes that the Hebrew for a two-edged sword is literally mouth mouths. On the judgment written Ellicott offers three possibilities without choosing: that it was some special order whose contents we could guess if we knew the exact circumstance that produced the psalm and had the names of the captured princes; or that it means the judgments registered here and there in the sacred books and so made legitimate by prescription; or that it bears a still more general sense. He then proposes a repunctuation, so that the line reads as an execution of judgment upon them, followed by a separate declaration that it is written that this honour belongs to all his saints. Clarke, having refused the theocratic reading, ends on a grim history: Israel had this honour while it continued faithful, and when it relapsed its enemies prevailed, the city was taken and the temple burnt, more than a million were slaughtered and the rest led captive and scattered.
